title: Weight Converter
context: Grade 3, the second weight topic of the metric measures chapter. An adult sees a rule being applied, multiply by one thousand and divide by one thousand. What is actually being settled is what one kilogram is made of and what a weight written in two units means: a child who has only the rule will move the digits the wrong way, will write a weight such as two kilograms ninety grams as twenty ninety grams, and will compare 1 kg 620 g with 1700 g by looking at the first digit. The tool breaks a real kilogram into its grams and lays the columns out.

writeup.why: Change kilograms into grams and grams into kilograms by seeing a kilogram bag break into a thousand grams and gather back, change a weight in kilograms and grams, and add and subtract weights in columns with a carry or a borrow.
writeup.look: A kitchen scale with a kilogram dial and a gram dial, a real bag of salt that pours out a thousand gram marks inside a vermilion ring, a Given tag, an Answer tag, a column board with a kilograms column and a grams column, and two shopping baskets.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Weight Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many conversions or sums have been worked. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A kitchen scale stands at the left, 300 across at x 90, y 220, with a round kilogram dial and a round gram dial side by side on its face, each 110 across, and a real white paper bag of salt labelled 1 kg on its pan. Beside it the kilogram stepper at x 90, y 540 (300 by 60) sets from 1 to 20 kilograms, and the grams stepper under it at x 90, y 610 (300 by 60) adds a number of grams for a weight in kilograms and grams. The Pour and Gather buttons stand at x 90, y 690 and x 250, y 690, each 150 by 56 and labelled in words. When Pour is pressed each kilogram bag opens and pours out its thousand gram marks, drawn as ten small paper bags of 100 g, each cut into ten tens, into a tray at x 420, y 230 (560 by 300) inside a vermilion ring labelled Unit fact, 1 kg = 1000 g. Gather runs it backwards, the gram marks flowing back into kilogram bags, one bag for every thousand, with a leftover of fewer than a thousand staying on the tray as grams. A deep blue Given tag at x 420, y 560 (260 by 60) names the weight the question gives, a green Answer tag at x 700, y 560 (260 by 60) names the weight the working reaches, and an amber Second tag at x 560, y 640 (240 by 56) holds the grams added on, each with its unit beside its number. On the fourth phase the column board replaces the tray: a board 520 by 280 at x 420, y 220 with two columns, kilograms and grams, headed in words, the first weight in the top row, the second weight one row under it, a short level line under them and the answer row below, with a small carried one drawn above the kilograms column and a borrowed kilogram broken into a thousand grams above the grams column. The two shopping baskets stand at x 960 and x 1060, y 220, each a basket of fruit in natural colours about 90 across, and a Basket button under each sets it on the scale. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing the converted weight, the sum or the difference into the answer slot. On the first phase the answer slot asks for grams, and on the second for kilograms. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours, and the chapter's four roles are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate, labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag, labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from sit inside a vermilion ring, labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag, labelled Second or Left. Every ruler mark, scale mark and plain edge is near-black, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of the four, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a measure is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The scale shows the last weight in both units, the bag poured out into its grams inside the vermilion ring, and the column board with its carry or borrow.

writeup.delight: On the first phase, the moment Pour is pressed, the bag of salt tips and the grams run out in ten small bags that each split into ten tens, inside the vermilion ring, and the kilogram dial turns to zero while the gram dial climbs. On the fourth phase a borrowed kilogram snaps into a thousand gram marks that slide across into the grams column.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase the kitchen scale holds a closed bag of salt and the kilogram stepper is set, with a vermilion ring waiting beside it. On the second a heap of gram marks lies on the scale, the Gather button is lit, and empty kilogram bags wait beside it. On the third the scale reads a weight in kilograms and grams, a Given tag names it, and an empty amber Second tag waits. On the fourth the column board is up with two weights written one under the other and two baskets of fruit beside it. One thing moves, once: the Pour button, or the first column on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any whole number of kilograms from one to twenty on the pan, the Pour and Gather buttons, a weight in kilograms and grams, the column board and the two baskets. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on a bag of salt, a bicycle, a parcel, a desk, a school backpack, a sack of flour and two baskets of fruit, changing both ways, kilograms and grams together, a zero in the grams, a borrowed kilogram, and which basket weighs more.
voiceLines: A kitchen scale and a bag of salt. Let us see what is inside a kilogram.
One kilogram pours out a thousand grams. How many grams does this weight pour out?
Every thousand grams make one kilogram. How many kilograms are in this heap?
Change the kilograms first. Then add the grams that are left. What is the weight in grams?
Work the grams first. Do the grams reach a thousand, or are there too few? Then the kilograms.
A new weight on the scale. Which unit does it start in?
Free play. Pour, gather and add any weights you like.
Look at the grams again. How many thousands are there? Then the grams that are left.
You changed kilograms and grams both ways, and you worked the columns grams first.

source_tool.description: A kitchen scale with a round dial in kilograms and a second round dial in grams stands at the left of the working area, 300 across, with a real bag of salt on its pan, a natural white paper packet labelled 1 kg. Beside it a number stepper sets how many kilograms are on the pan, from 1 to 20. Each kilogram bag opens when the Pour button is pressed and pours out a thousand gram marks, drawn as ten small bags of 100 g, each bag cut into ten tens, inside a vermilion ring labelled Unit fact, 1 kg = 1000 g, so a kilogram is seen to be a thousand grams and three kilograms three thousands. A Gather button runs the other way: the gram marks flow back into kilogram bags, one bag for every thousand, and a leftover of fewer than a thousand stays as grams. A Given tag in deep blue names the weight the question gives and an Answer tag in green names the weight the working reaches, with the unit beside every number. For a weight in kilograms and grams the child changes the kilograms first, in the vermilion ring, and then adds the grams in an amber tag labelled Second. A column board with two columns, kilograms and grams, takes two weights one under the other, the grams column worked first, with a small carried one drawn above the kilograms column when the grams reach a thousand and a borrowed kilogram broken into a thousand grams above the grams column when the top grams are too few. Two real shopping baskets, each a basket of fruit in natural colours, can be set on the scale one after the other, and the child must change both weights to one unit before the scale says which basket holds more. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many conversions or sums have been worked.
source_tool.art_direction: A kitchen counter with a real scale / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a ruler, a measuring tape, a metre rod, a paper clip, a pencil, a book, a door, a ribbon, mangoes, a loaf of bread, potatoes, a bag of salt, a two pan balance with iron weights, a kitchen scale, measuring jugs, a glass, a teacup, a bucket, a bottle, a pot, a juice packet. The object is the thing the child measures, weighs or pours, and a plain bar or tank appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every scale is drawn with its marks evenly spaced and its zero at the edge: a ruler from 0, a metre rod in ten equal tens, a jug in equal marks, a balance with its beam level or tilted by the true difference. A reading is always taken at a mark, never between two.

Every unit is written next to its number, and a number is never written bare where a unit belongs. A unit fact is shown with both its sides, so 1 m = 100 cm is one object and one hundred centimetre marks side by side.

Converting is something the child does: a metre rod breaks into a hundred centimetre marks, a kilogram bag pours out a thousand gram dots, a litre jug empties into a thousand millilitre drops. The vermilion ring carries the times 100 or times 1000 step while it happens.
A sum or a difference is laid out in columns, units over their column, the second amount directly under the first, with a carried amount shown above the column it joins.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance. Large amounts are shown as a few tens, hundreds or thousands.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a mark or a reading the child is looking at, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a mango stays yellow and a metal weight stays dark grey. The four roles of the chapter are carried by what holds the object or the number, never by tinting the object. The measure the question gives, or the reading taken from the ruler, the balance or the jug, sits in a deep blue tag or on a deep blue plate and is labelled Given. The measure the working reaches, a converted or total amount, sits in a green tag and is labelled Answer. The times 100 or times 1000 step and the unit fact it comes from, such as one metre is one hundred centimetres, sit inside a vermilion ring and are labelled Unit fact. The second amount of a sum or a difference, an amount carried and a part left over sit in an amber tag and are labelled Second or Left. Those four are the same four in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Every ruler mark, scale mark, outline and plain edge is near-black, and the stage still reads with the colour taken away because each role is named in writing first.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the grams again. How many thousands are there? Then the grams that are left.
voice.onNext: A new weight on the scale. Which unit does it start in?
voice.opening: A kitchen scale and a bag of salt. Let us see what is inside a kilogram.
voice.onFinish: You changed kilograms and grams both ways, and you worked the columns grams first.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Pour, gather and add any weights you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has weighed a kilogram of rice on a kitchen scale and shared it into small bags of a hundred grams by hand, counting ten bags. The tool is what pours a thousand grams out of a bag without a mess, runs the pour backwards, and shows a kilogram broken for a borrow, which a real bag of rice cannot do in front of the child.

answer_key.rule: One kilogram is one thousand grams. To change kilograms into grams, multiply by one thousand. To change grams into kilograms, divide by one thousand. A weight in kilograms and grams is changed to grams by changing the kilograms first and then adding the grams, and a zero in the hundreds place of the grams must be kept, so 2 kg 90 g is 2090 g. Weights are added and subtracted like ordinary numbers with the unit kept, and weights in kilograms and grams are written in two columns and worked grams first. When the grams add to a thousand or more, a kilogram is carried to the kilograms column, and when the top grams are fewer than the grams taken away, one kilogram is broken into a thousand grams. Two weights are compared only when they are in the same unit.
answer_key.wrong: The bag opens again slowly and the gram marks are counted out one hundred at a time, or the column board is shown again with the grams column worked first and the carry or borrow drawn above it. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: One kilogram is one thousand grams.
2 kg is 2 lots of one thousand grams.
Multiply the kilograms by one thousand.
So 2 kg is two thousand grams.

steps: Change the kilograms first: 4 kg is four thousand grams.
items.question: A parcel weighs 4 kg 700 g. How many grams is that?
items.checkpoint: Change the kilograms first, then add the grams.
items.misconception: Writing 4 kg 700 g as 47000 g, by pushing the two numbers together with a zero too many.

steps: Write the kilograms in one column and the grams in another.
Add the grams: 650 g plus 140 g is 790 g.
Add the kilograms: 2 kg plus 1 kg is 3 kg.
So the basket holds 3 kg 790 g.
items.question: A basket holds 2 kg 650 g of apples and 1 kg 140 g of oranges. How much fruit is in the basket?
items.checkpoint: Add the grams column first, then the kilograms column, and keep the unit.
items.misconception: Adding all four numbers as one sum, which mixes grams and kilograms.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A bag of salt weighs 1 kg. How many grams is that?
A parcel weighs 19000 g. How many kilograms is that?
items.final_answer: 19 kg, because 19000 divided by one thousand is 19

items.question: A school backpack weighs 1 kg 120 g. How many grams is that?
items.final_answer: 1120 g, because one kilogram is one thousand grams and one thousand plus 120 is 1120

items.question: A bag of rice weighs 3 kg and a bag of flour weighs 2 kg. What do they weigh together?
items.final_answer: 5 kg, because 3 kg plus 2 kg is 5 kg

items.question: A desk weighs 29000 g. How many kilograms is that?
items.final_answer: 29 kg, because 29000 divided by one thousand is 29

items.question: A bag of oranges weighs 2 kg 90 g. How many grams is that?
items.final_answer: 2090 g, because 2 kg is two thousand grams and the 90 g goes after it with a zero kept, so the answer is 2090 g and not 290 g

items.question: A sack of flour weighs 5 kg 140 g. A baker uses 2 kg 380 g. How much flour is left?
items.final_answer: 2 kg 760 g, because 140 g is fewer than 380 g, so one kilogram is changed into one thousand grams, and 1140 g minus 380 g is 760 g and 4 kg minus 2 kg is 2 kg

items.question: One child buys 1 kg of bananas and 620 g of oranges. Another child buys 1700 g of watermelon. Who buys more fruit?
items.final_answer: The child who buys the watermelon, because 1 kg 620 g is 1620 g and 1620 g is less than 1700 g

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: sets how many kilograms of salt are on the pan, from 1 to 20
opens each kilogram bag and pours out a thousand gram marks inside the vermilion ring
runs the pour backwards, gram marks flowing back into kilogram bags
adds a number of grams to the kilograms for a weight in kilograms and grams
takes two weights one under the other, the grams column worked first, with a carry or borrow above
set one shopping basket or the other on the scale
types the converted weight, or a sum or difference, into the answer slot

teaching_notes: Weigh a kilogram of rice on a kitchen scale before the tool opens and share it into small bags of a hundred grams by hand, counting ten of them, so that a thousand grams is a kilogram that has been counted. Say the unit with every number, a number of kilograms and a number of grams, and never a bare number. For kilograms and grams together, write the two parts with a gap between them and ask for the grams in three places, so that a weight such as two kilograms ninety grams keeps its zero. In the columns, ask which column to work first and why: the grams, because they might reach a thousand. When two weights are in different units, ask what must be done before they are compared. Use fresh numbers: the exercise's weights and its three fruits are the child's to change and add.
generation_prompt: Build a weight conversion tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, drawn from real everyday objects as recognisable flat illustrations in their own natural colours, with no photographs and no people. A kitchen scale about 300 across stands at the left of the working area with a round kilogram dial and a round gram dial and a white paper bag of salt labelled 1 kg on its pan, and a number stepper sets from 1 to 20 kilograms. A Pour button opens each kilogram bag and pours out a thousand gram marks drawn as ten small bags of 100 g, each cut into ten tens, inside a vermilion ring labelled Unit fact, 1 kg = 1000 g, and a Gather button runs it backwards, gram marks flowing into kilogram bags with a leftover under a thousand staying as grams. A Given tag in deep blue names the weight the question gives, an Answer tag in green the weight the working reaches, and an amber Second tag holds the grams added to changed kilograms. A column board with a kilograms column and a grams column takes two weights one under the other, grams worked first, drawing a carried one above the kilograms column and a borrowed kilogram broken into a thousand grams above the grams column. Two real baskets of fruit in natural colours can be set on the scale, and both weights must be changed to one unit before the scale says which is more. The running count at the top left of the canvas is how many conversions or sums have been worked. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Set the kilograms and press Pour. Press Gather to turn grams back into kilograms. Work the grams column first. Change both weights to one unit before you compare them.
